finding.claim: delete_file calls is_allowed (imported under the alias require_allowed) and discards the boolean result, so no authorization is enforced. Any caller can delete any file. The name 'require_allowed' suggests it enforces, but it only returns True/False. ensure_allowed (which aborts 403) was intended.
finding.source: Any HTTP client sending DELETE /files/<fid> with any or no X-Session-User-Verified header; fid is attacker-chosen

trace.note: is_allowed imported as require_allowed, a misleading alias for a non-enforcing predicate
f = STORE[fid] looks up the resource by attacker-supplied id
require_allowed(...) returns a bool that is ignored, so there is no abort
is_allowed only returns a bool and never raises

finding.guards_checked: ensure_allowed would abort(403) but is not used on this route. The before_request hook only sets g.user and does not reject. No other auth decorators or middleware exist in the repo. The result of the is_allowed call is not checked.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: before_request load_user (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user; ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 but is only used on rename_file (views.py:26), not delete_file
verdict.reason: views.py:4 aliases the bool-returning is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) as require_allowed, and views.py:18 calls it as a bare statement with the result discarded, so views.py:19 `del STORE[fid]` runs for any anonymous caller who supplies an existing fid (a missing fid only causes a KeyError/500 at views.py:17).

verdict_facts.reason: views.py:18 calls require_allowed, which is aliased to the bool-returning is_allowed (views.py:4, acl.py:4-5), and discards the result, so views.py:19 `del STORE[fid]` runs for any caller who supplies a valid fid; the before_request hook (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user and never rejects.

finding.claim: The user identity is taken straight from a client-supplied request header (X-Session-User-Verified), with no session, signature or token verification. Despite the name, nothing verifies it. Any client can impersonate any user listed in a resource's grants, so the ACL check in rename_file is bypassed by sending the owner's name. This is only safe if a trusted upstream proxy strips and sets this header, and nothing in the code enforces that.
finding.source: X-Session-User-Verified HTTP request header, fully attacker-controlled
finding.sink: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "write") at views.py:26, leading to the rename write at views.py:27 (also the delete check)

trace.note: g.user is passed to the ACL check as the principal
is_allowed looks up grants[user] using the spoofed name

finding.guards_checked: There is no signature, session or JWT validation in this repo. No proxy-trust or header-stripping logic is visible. The header may be set by a gateway outside this code, which would make this mitigated, so it depends on deployment. If the header is absent, g.user is None and grants.get(None) is empty, so anonymous callers are denied on rename.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts with 403 if is_allowed is false, but it only checks grants for the supplied user string. Nothing authenticates that string. Anonymous requests give None, which is denied. No signature, session, or proxy-trust check exists in the repo.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 sets g.user from the client-controlled X-Session-User-Verified header with no verification, so sending a granted user's name passes ensure_allowed at views.py:26 (acl.py:5, 9-10) and reaches the write at views.py:27. Exploitability depends on whether an upstream gateway strips and sets the header, which this code does not enforce. Separately, delete_file (views.py:18) calls is_allowed aliased as require_allowed and discards the result, so delete has no ACL enforcement at all.

verdict_facts.guard_found: No in-code control: no signature, session or proxy-trust check. The acl.py:8-10 ensure_allowed aborts with 403 correctly. It only checks the principal taken from the header, and grants.get(None) denies anonymous callers.
verdict_facts.reason: The trace is accurate (views.py:12 copies the header into g.user, views.py:26 and acl.py:5 use it as the principal, views.py:27 writes), but whether a client can forge X-Session-User-Verified depends on whether an upstream gateway strips and sets it, which this directory doesn't show. Separately, views.py:18 discards the bool from is_allowed (aliased as require_allowed), so DELETE has no ACL enforcement at all. That is a different bug from this finding.

finding.claim: STORE[fid] raises KeyError for a nonexistent id, producing a 500. In rename_file, request.json['name'] on a missing or invalid body also errors. Both are low-severity robustness issues. The 403-vs-500 difference also lets callers enumerate which file IDs exist, because the lookup runs before the authz check.

trace.note: the authz check happens only after the existence lookup, so the response differs between existing (403) and non-existing (500) ids
request.json['name'] is unvalidated, with no type or length check

finding.guards_checked: No error handlers are registered. STORE is a global in-memory dict with no per-tenant scoping.

verdict.guard_found: none for the KeyError/enumeration. Only ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, aborts 403) at views.py:26, and it runs after the STORE lookup. No error handlers are registered.
verdict.reason: views.py:17 and :25 do an unguarded STORE[fid] before the authz check at views.py:26, and :27 reads request.json["name"] unvalidated, so a missing id gives 500 and an existing id without grants gives 403, which is an existence oracle. This is low severity. Separately, and more serious than this finding: delete_file at views.py:18 calls require_allowed, which is an alias for the bool-returning is_allowed (views.py:4, acl.py:4), and discards the result, so DELETE is never authorized.

verdict_facts.guard_found: none (no error handlers or 404 handling; ensure_allowed at views.py:26 runs only after the STORE lookup)
verdict_facts.reason: views.py:17 and :25 use STORE[fid] before any authz, so an unknown id raises KeyError (500) while a known id without a grant gets 403 from acl.py:10, and views.py:27 reads request.json["name"] unvalidated; this is a real but low-severity robustness and ID-existence-oracle issue reachable by any caller. Separately, views.py:18 calls require_allowed, which is the bool-returning is_allowed with its result discarded, so delete_file does no authz check at all. That is a much more serious bug than this finding.
